In practice it remains a weapon of war, albeit below the threshold of kinetic force, to weaken a state by inhibiting its ability to achieve its strategic objectives. Specifically, POLWAR is the discipline, instruments and methods in which the political system of an adversary is the exclusive target to generate confusion, dissent, undermine relationships or influence policy decisions . As captured by Kennan, the 1948 US diplomat to the Soviet Union, POLWAR is considered a battle for influence using all the levers of national power below the threshold of war . In achieving this influence, the execution of POLWAR leverages diplomatic, economic, covert, informational and psychological means to apply pressure on an adversary’s political system to shape a particular outcome in favour of the POLWAR proponent . Its emergence in modern warfare is due, in part, to a shift in the context of conflict where national security is not based on defence against overt attack, but the threat of diminished global influence in achieving national objectives and maintaining sovereignty .
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: This is to say, Russia desires to position itself as a counter-balance to US dominance, providing alternative trade and economic value to, as example, the Middle-East that is not tethered to US primacy . Operationally, this requires the ability to undermine or inhibit the reach of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation without conflict and to generate instability in the states separating Russia and Europe . In this strategic objective, Russia targets both regional and international political systems with ever-increasing nuance and sophistication. Regionally, during the 2004 Ukrainian Presidential elections, the pro-independence and anti-Russian candidate Yushchenko was poisoned and disfigured by an unknown assailant . Unexpectedly surviving, Yushchenko continued to campaign, and on voting day masked men were reported at polling booths harassing and intimidating Yushchenko voters . Further, millions of votes were later attributed to long since deceased citizens, giving the pro-Russian Yanukovych the win . However, the crude methods of suspected Russian POLWAR activities were discovered and mass protests erupted, resulting in a second election ultimately handing power to Yushchenko .
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: However, these presumed Russian POLWAR tactics would soon be refined as highlighted in the following 2014 Ukrainian election, whereby voting machines were recoded to predetermine the vote count coordinated with an intensive information campaign announcing the leading and presumptive winner of the election ahead of official results . The objective of these activities was to influence undecided voters and provide an air of legitimacy to the fraudulent electronically tallied election results . Internationally, these same methods were detected in the 2016 US elections whereby compromise of the electoral system and an information campaign worked in tandem to achieve (presumed) Russian strategic objectives. It is suspected that the highly sophisticated information campaign aimed to escalate division in social groups and dominate media messaging to sway the election outcome against nominee Clinton; having had a history of tension with Russian President Putin . As an example of the utility of POLWAR, the middle power Iran has also adopted these methods to enhance their national security and propel their strategic agenda.
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: Further, through adopting POLWAR, Iran has generated a force-multiplier in rallying internal and external party factions, as well as regional neighbours, in resisting US influence to position itself as a leader against ‘US imperialism’ . Like Russia, Iran uses information warfare vectored through social media and sympathetic or controlled media outlets to influence social discourse and normalise its political messaging . However, Iran has also developed a strong network of proxy-state actors to provide a level of deniability for its actions as well as directly influence or generate events that serve a higher political, security or national objective . These actions are central to Iranian defence strategy, and as such Iran has developed or funded Iranian news broadcasting in 45 countries, five foreign-language broadcasting stations and over 70 ‘Iranian Cultural Centres’ across the globe in addition to 26 official embassies . These efforts have seen Iraqi and Iranian relations flourish and ties strengthen with Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Houthi controlled Yemen, establishing a regional resistance to US influence . Similarly, al-Qaeda, while not a nation state or commanding the same influence it once did, uses POLWAR tactics to influence and achieve strategic military ends.
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: Post the 9/11 attacks, the ability to influence the regional and religious narrative has been key in their strategy of resistance against stronger adversaries . The al-Qaeda POLWAR has two key objectives: undermine the authority and objectives of the enemy; and, in parallel, rally their people to the cause . Through leveraging religion and the ubiquity of the internet, al-Qaeda is able to broadcast the west’s departure from religious norms as well as emphasise and politically frame the west’s military interventions or mistakes. Through this method of POLWAR, al-Qaeda were successful in not only expanding their recruitment base to international levels but were also able to generate sympathisers within western political systems, reducing the resolve for continued war . In achieving this, great effort was placed in the curating of messages and visuals to undermine the legitimacy of Western nations and the righteousness of resistance, in a battle for hearts and minds, which in winning translated to operational support and mobility by the local population . As a result, POLWAR provided the vastly outgunned al-Qaeda a method that could control the perception of the people, and in doing so directly attack the political objectives of the US and Western allies.
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: These functions create a framework ‘to apply the principles and best practices of risk management to improving security and resilience’ . Moreover, the intrusion mechanisms and principles of exploitation outlined by NIST broadly correlate when examining POLWAR, notably reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery and exploitation . As a result, NIST’s principles of security are well structured to enable examination of Western military frameworks for planning and campaigning to identify, protect, detect and respond to POLWAR activities . In accordance with NIST, ‘Identify’ is defined as ‘understanding the business context [and] the resources that support critical functions’ . Further, ‘Protect’ is to ‘develop and implement appropriate safeguards to ensure delivery of critical services’, while ‘Detect’ is the development of systems to identify malign activities . In order to appropriately achieve these three functions as a counter to POLWAR, Western military planning frameworks would require mechanisms to highlight critical national and political functions. However, upon examination it becomes apparent that Western militaries are not designed or mandated to achieve this, and as such are not appropriately empowered.
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: In understanding the militaries legislative restrictions, and its role as a responsive action, examination must turn to how Western militaries obtain their authority to commence planning and response action. As a definition, ‘Respond’ calls for the ability to ‘develop and implement appropriate activities to take action’ . In this, the United States Joint Planning Doctrine outlines four explicit phases of planning: Strategic Guidance, Concept Development, Plan Development and Plan Assessment . The first aspect of this process, strategic guidance, outlines where the US military receives its authority and direction for the execution of military force, namely the President of the United States . While the military is enabled to provide guidance to the President through the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, it is not empowered to operate without the President’s explicit authority . This command structure highlights that the US Military would require external mechanisms to detect POLWAR activities and then require the political powers to determine military force as an appropriate response measure to initiate a military planning process .
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: In considering the deprivation of political authority, such actions need not be overt or hostile and need only to disincentivise military—or any—action to be effective. This is to say that nullifying the activation of the military can be achieved through implied threat of economic hardship, invoking Western legal protections or, more importantly, undermining political will. To clarify, for Australia, the mechanism for the military to name and engage an enemy can be achieved by an act of Cabinet, without consent of Parliament or the Queen’s vested Executive Power in the Governor-General . Such power exists under the Defence Act 1903, Section 50C; however, any member of Government can table the matter for debate and make any use of, or the intent to use, military force public knowledge . In understanding this, for the military to counter POLWAR and initiate a defence it would require the Cabinet of the day to, in effect, openly declare an intent to do so. This declaration brings with it public scrutiny and debate—providing an additional POLWAR platform for the adversary. Such public scrutiny is of little consequence to nations such as Russia and Iran, having made countering Western influence a cultural cornerstone of national politics.
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: However, for Australia and other Western nations, declaring an intent to attack a nation, politically or otherwise, is a more difficult proposition as it provides the target nation justifiable retaliatory or defensive measures under the United Nations Charter, Article 51. Specifically, it provides the target nation justification in using response measures for self-defence and the ability to seek sanctions under the rules of the World Trade Organisation . As a result, Western nations are seemingly trapped by their own rules-based order. In short, if western nations wish to harness the military in response to, or conducting, POLWAR, its disclosure is inevitable and provides advantage to the adversary. The critical vulnerability of political authority notwithstanding, once the military is authorised as a response action its ability to plan and execute defensive or offensive action is robust. Specifically, Australia’s Campaign Cycle, as outlined in Joint Planning ADDP 5.0, allows for the identification and alignment of national strategic and military strategic objectives executed through the operational planning and tactical capabilities of military force . Moreover, the Campaign Cycle of campaign design and management is adaptable and incorporates assessment and adaptation phases to ensure that execution is meeting intended strategic outcomes .
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

text: Further, such planning empowers the military to draw on whole-of-government capability and powers to execute a campaign or operation, representing the first formal mechanism by which Australia can generate a whole-of-government response to POLWAR . Moreover, in response to the critical flaw of political authority over military execution at the national strategic level, the existing frameworks are insulated from this at the military strategic level down through to the tactical level of execution . This is to say, the command and control of approved military activity is the sole remit of the Australia Defence Force . In theory this separation insulates military operational and tactical activities from any effects of adversary POLWAR directed towards government. Such flexibility is also reflected in other Western military campaign planning, for example the US Joint Doctrine Note 1-19, Competition Continuum. The doctrine note describes a campaign planning environment as ‘a world of enduring competition conducted through a mixture of cooperation, competition below armed conflict, and armed conflict’ . In this, it outlines that a campaign can execute and engage an enemy at different stages of a campaign, or concurrently at different levels of the continuum, to achieve the strategic objective .
title: Political Warfare: Where Do We Stand?

Introduction Clausewitz defines the concept of the centre of gravity (COG) as ‘the hub of all power and movement, on which everything depends. That is the point against which all our energies should be directed’. Military planners across the Western world have recognised the importance of this concept, capturing it in military planning doctrine. Australia is no exception and first incorporated COG as a concept in 1998, and more recently, detailing the criticality of the centre of gravity within the Australian Defence Force Procedure 5.0.1 – Joint Military Appreciation Process (herein referred to as JMAP). Joseph Strange, a professor of strategic studies, and Colonel Richard Iron, British Army, define the centre of gravity as ‘the primary entity that possesses the inherent capability to achieve an objective or the desired end state’, which the JMAP has adopted. Despite the recognised importance of the centre of gravity, the JMAP nests the derivation and analysis of the centres of gravity within the broader process of Mission Analysis. The implication is that the importance of the centre of gravity, as a sub-step, is obscured in favour of conducting the superior processes within the JMAP.
title: Moving the Centre of Gravity; from a Linear process to a Systems-of-Systems approach

text: The ADF’s centre-of-gravity process would benefit from an investment in advanced technologies and AI models centred on the JMAP to create a complex adaptive system. This would allow for a dynamic and sophisticated planning tool that can handle fluid environments and provide timely inputs into operational missions.

To improve how the ADF identifies key factors in planning, they should use better technology and artificial intelligence. This would help planners make smarter decisions faster by adapting to changing situations and providing more accurate information.

This essay will then argue that embedded critical and design thinking will enhance the analysis and development of the ADF’s centres of gravity and avoid a checklist approach to operational planning. Modern warfare is becoming increasingly complex, and Australian doctrine must provide a centre-of-gravity process that is deeply considered, non-linear and adaptable to emerging conditions. As such, the essay will argue that the JMAP risks driving a linear checklist approach to the centre-of-gravity analysis, delivering a campaign plan that is ‘mechanistic, reductionist and inadequate for an increasingly complex battlespace and array of missions’. Defining the centre of gravity in a JMAP context The JMAP’s definition of a centre of gravity relies on Dr Joseph L. Strange and Colonel Richard Iron’s interpretation of Clausewitz’s description of the centre-of-gravity concept. Strange and Iron argue that centres of gravity are not limited to physical characteristics, capabilities, or locations, nor is a centre of gravity a single ‘hub of all power and movement’. Instead, they provide a nuanced approach of ‘dynamic and powerful physical and moral agents of action or influence with certain qualities and capabilities that derive their benefit from a given location or terrain’.
title: Moving the Centre of Gravity; from a Linear process to a Systems-of-Systems approach

text: The ADF’s centre-of-gravity process would benefit from an investment in advanced technologies and AI models centred on the JMAP that genuinely provides a complex adaptive system. As early as 2002, George Mason University and the US Army War College were exploring the creation of an AI system synergised with military strategy research to support centre-of-gravity analysis. Their experimentation significantly improved the centre-of-gravity analysis, with the system learning and adapting from previous inputs. It delivered a model that gave subsequent users highly reasoned centre-of-gravity candidates for consideration. Over the following two decades, computing technologies and AI have achieved enormous improvements, automating many processes that would have previously relied on a ‘human in the loop’, as the JMAP still does. title: Moving the Centre of Gravity; from a Linear process to a Systems-of-Systems approach

text: The continued utility of the centre-of-gravity analysis has been questioned, with fears that an entrenched doctrinal approach and organisational norms have limited the level of cognitive investment by planners. This has led to calls for the centre of gravity to be discarded as a planning tool as it hampers deep thinking and experimentation. Design thinking is just one alternative that has been offered. As a concept, design thinking struggles with a single definition that caters to the diversity of ideas and methods under its label. Design thinking seeks to ‘connect and integrate useful knowledge from the arts and sciences alike, but in ways that are suited to the problems and purposes of the present’. This essay argues that discarding the centre of gravity from the JMAP risks losing the required uniformity to support a system-of-systems approach. Applying design thinking could benefit the centre-of-gravity analysis and development process. As a sub-step in centre-of-gravity analysis, the addition of design thinking could assist in disrupting the JMAP’s current static behaviours through an epistemological frame as proposed by Dr Ben Zweibelson, Director of Design Programs for the United States Joint Special Operations University.
title: Moving the Centre of Gravity; from a Linear process to a Systems-of-Systems approach

text: Zweibelson contends that the current joint planning processes are ill-equipped for complex systems, such as the complex operational environments the ADF may face. Horst Rittel, a design theorist, developed the ‘wicked problem’, a concept that the JMAP could adopt. Buchanan has drawn on Rittel’s properties of wicked problems to note that there are no definitive conditions or limits to design problems such as the centre-of-gravity analysis. Together, these approaches are ways to overcome an entrenched doctrinal approach to achieve creative and highly developed centres of gravity. The application of critical and design thinking to the centre-of-gravity analysis and development is currently challenged by the JMAP’s linear centre-of-gravity process and simplistic examples. The JMAP’s hypothetical example of a centre of gravity is highly reductive.
title: Moving the Centre of Gravity; from a Linear process to a Systems-of-Systems approach

text: Gone is the ‘steamroller with which one can flatten all problems in the same way’, replaced with an ADF planner with the ‘adroitness of a puppeteer, who at one time holds many strings in his hands and who is able to adapt his movements to the given circumstances in the most sophisticated ways’. The approach to understanding the operational environment used in JMAP and by AI have similarities. Both seek to create a model of reality. In JMAP this model is instantiated in the biological brains of planners, aided by various cognitive artifacts such as diagrams, maps, and written text. text: Theoretical Applicability To analyse their applicability to the ADF, I consider the theoretical aspects of how JMAP and AI-enhanced planning might be applied by a military organisation. Knorr-Cetina studies the behaviour of expert systems in science, showing how the conduct of certain activities shapes and changes an organisation. text: Although her research focused on scientific laboratories as knowledge organisations, she conceded that the notion of epistemic cultures could be applied ‘to expert cultures outside science’. I consider that a headquarters engaged in planning can exhibit distributed cognition, and exploring the notion of ‘distributed cognition’ further helps us understand how to consider the role of AI in planning. The notion of distributed cognition allows me to assess the applicability of AI and the JMAP to the ADF. Vaesen summarises the theory by saying: ‘The basic idea behind distributed cognition (d-cog) is that cognition often distributes across individuals and/or epistemic aids such as instruments, diagrams, calculators, computers, and so forth. Hutchins famously illustrates distributed cognition with the example of a ship navigating into port. After extensive study aboard US Navy ships, he came to conclude that the system of humans and instruments together direct the ship. This system achieved cognitive results outside any one human mind, and more than the sum of the individual cognition of each human in the process. Seeing AI in this manner reveals that it is merely another non-human element in a system that already integrates various cognitive artifacts.

Further, as military headquarters already distribute cognition between humans and artifacts, there is no theoretical obstacle to AI integration. text: During Vice Admiral Peter Jones' tenure as President from 2015 to 2023, the Australian Naval Institute experienced significant financial and sponsorship developments. In 2015, the Institute had an operating loss and faced financial instability, but by 2023, despite a one-off operating loss of $34,000 due to the Defence Strategic Review, it maintained a generally healthy financial position. The Institute increased its sponsorship base from nine companies in 2015 to 14 in 2023, including new sponsors such as Serco, Luerssen, Kongsberg, and Systematic, while retaining long-term supporters. This enabled the Institute to continue its activities unamended and maintain its value proposition to sponsors.

While Vice Admiral Peter Jones was President from 2015 to 2023, the Australian Naval Institute went through some financial ups and downs. In 2015, the Institute had a loss, but by 2023, it was in a better financial position overall, even though it had a $34,000 loss one year because of the Defence Strategic Review. The Institute also grew its list of supporters, going from nine companies in 2015 to 14 in 2023, including new names like Serco, Luerssen, Kongsberg, and Systematic. The Institute kept its activities going and stayed valuable to its supporters.

The Fairmile Type B Motor Launches were the first volume production class, with 383 units built. They measured 112 feet in length, displaced 85 tonnes, and had an endurance of 1500 nautical miles at 12 knots with a maximum speed of 20 knots. These vessels served in multiple roles including as Motor Torpedo Boats, Motor Gun Boats, rescue craft, navigation leaders, minelayers, and minesweepers.

The Fairmile Type B boats were the first large batch made, with 383 built. They were 112 feet long, weighed 85 tonnes, and could travel 1500 miles at 12 knots with a top speed of 20 knots. They were used for various jobs like attacking enemy ships, rescuing people, leading navigation, laying mines, and clearing mines.

The Australian military observer, as a UNMO, provided spontaneous commentary on the post-referendum process, including the role of the government and UN agencies until the Timorese government was capable of taking over. The observer's remarks were well-received by the local population.

An Australian military observer working with the UN gave an off-the-cuff talk about what would happen after the referendum, including the roles of the government and UN agencies until Timor-Leste could take over. The talk was well-received by the local people.

Arctis offers information access controls that allow policies to be set dynamically against data, solving the zero trust problem as defined by the new compliance frameworks enforced by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in the U.S.

Arctis provides tools to control who can access data and how, with policies that can be adjusted as needed. These tools help meet the latest security standards, like the zero trust approach promoted in the U.S.

China's expanding security engagement in the Pacific and Indian Ocean regions is reshaping the Indo-Pacific strategic environment by enabling Beijing to build familiarity with operating environments, normalise its presence, and pursue strategic objectives beyond its home waters. This includes regular and geographically distributed activities involving naval task groups, CCG vessels, research platforms, and maritime militia, which contribute to a denser operating environment, routine encounters, and increased risk of miscalculation.

China is increasing its security presence in the Pacific and Indian Ocean regions, which is changing how the area is strategically managed. By regularly sending military and support vessels, China is becoming more familiar with the region and normalising its presence. This leads to more frequent interactions and raises the risk of misunderstandings or accidental conflicts.

Australia and India working in concert would be able to maintain the independence and stability of the area, providing sufficient impetus for India to join a coalition, at least informally. This alignment supports India's strategic purpose and enables a loosely built coalition of major Asian powers to exert economic, diplomatic, and military deterrence to control the region and maintain peace.

If Australia and India work together in the Indian Ocean, they can help keep the area stable and independent. This partnership would encourage India to join a coalition, at least informally, and support India's goals. Together, they can use economic, diplomatic, and military pressure to maintain peace in the region.

The central focus of Noam Chomsky's book 'Failed States' is a sustained critique of United States foreign policy and its internal democratic shortcomings, including unilateral use of force, disregard for international law, and the influence of special interest lobbies that undermine democratic processes.

The main focus of Noam Chomsky's book 'Failed States' is to criticize US foreign policy and how the US government acts alone in using military force, ignores international rules, and lets powerful groups influence decisions, which weakens democracy.

The Battle of the Coral Sea inflicted damage on the Japanese Navy that made the subsequent strategic victory at Midway possible. It also prevented the Japanese from seizing Port Moresby, which was critical for Australia's ability to provide a base for US Forces.
The Battle of the Coral Sea weakened the Japanese Navy and stopped them from taking Port Moresby, which was important for supporting US forces in the Pacific.

WO1 Wally Thompson was a suitable candidate for his appointment as WO1-A due to his three tours of Vietnam, mentions in dispatches, combat wounds, and awards. He demonstrated courage, initiative, and teamwork, and was known for leading by example. His role allowed him to provide a soldiers’ perspective to the Chief of General Staff and communicate strategic direction to the ranks.

Wally Thompson was a good fit for his role because he had served in Vietnam three times, was recognized for his bravery, and had been wounded in combat. He was known for being courageous, working well with others, and leading by example. In his position, he could share soldiers' experiences with top leaders and help pass on important messages to the troops.

The collaboration between Australia and Northrop Grumman has fostered a symbiotic relationship where Australia's early engagement and conceptual contributions have influenced the evolution of UAV capabilities. This includes the successful utilisation of Australian concepts by the US and the confidence gained from initial trials, which demonstrated Australia's valued role in shaping future capabilities such as the Triton system.

Working together with Northrop Grumman has helped Australia shape the development of drone technology. Australia's early ideas and testing have influenced how these drones are designed and used, and the US has used some of Australia's ideas. This has built confidence in the program and led to successful projects like the Triton.

The Regulations outlined specific responsibilities for junior leaders, including captains, lieutenants, and ensigns. Captains were to ensure the health, discipline, and welfare of their men, foster attachment through kindness, and personally visit the sick. Lieutenants were to promote health and convenience, inspect living conditions, and manage complaints. Ensigns were tasked with ensuring the cleanliness and order of soldiers' appearance and equipment during parades.

The rules set out what junior leaders like captains, lieutenants, and ensigns should do. Captains needed to look after their soldiers' health and discipline, be kind, and visit the sick. Lieutenants had to check how soldiers were living, make sure their food was good, and help with their complaints. Ensigns were in charge of making sure soldiers were clean and well-dressed during parades.

Allan Dundas worked on upgrades to advanced electronic support measure systems and early electronic countermeasures capabilities, including those integrated into the F-111 aircraft. These systems utilised digital RF memories to jam radars and significantly enhanced surveillance and self-protection capabilities.

Allan Dundas worked on improving early electronic warfare systems, like those used in the F-111 plane. These systems helped detect and disrupt radar signals and were some of the first of their kind in the country.

The Australian presence at RMAF Butterworth has provided strategic and operational benefits including enhanced jungle warfighting skills, strengthened relationships with Malaysian and Singaporean partners, preparation for operational deployments such as to the Solomon Islands, and the contribution of highly motivated and well-trained soldiers to the permanent force. Additionally, it has enabled rapid ADF responses during contingency operations such as Operation VISTA and Operation SUMATRA ASSIST, and supported RAAF surveillance missions in the North Indian Ocean and South China Sea, contributing to regional security and stability.

Being at RMAF Butterworth has helped Australian soldiers improve their skills in jungle warfare, build good relationships with Malaysia and Singapore, and get ready for other missions like going to the Solomon Islands. It also helped bring more trained soldiers into the regular army. The base was useful for helping during evacuations and humanitarian aid after a big tsunami, and it allowed Australian planes to monitor important areas of the ocean. This shows the value of the partnership with Malaysia and supports regional security.

The Australian Defence Force is currently facing significant challenges in determining what not to fund as it pivots in response to the Defence Strategic Review. This process is draining energy, morale, and focus, with a lot of work still required to clarify what will and will not be supported. The pivot has exposed weaknesses in capability that need to be addressed to align with the new direction and focus.

The Australian Defence Force is struggling to decide which programs to cut as it adjusts to the Defence Strategic Review. This is causing a lot of stress and uncertainty, and there's still a lot of work to be done before it's clear what will be supported. The changes have revealed some gaps in what the Defence Force can do, which need to be fixed to match the new goals.

Operational planning for long-range patrolling in New Guinea must account for the patrol's primary tasks, such as gathering military information, training in operational roles, and engaging with local populations to gain goodwill. Route planning is critical, as patrols typically follow established village tracks or hunting paths due to unreliable maps, and rely on compass, sun, and local knowledge for navigation. Given the isolation and limited communication, commanders must ensure adequate pre-planning, including sufficient supplies and route information, as resupply and additional support are not readily available.

When planning patrols in New Guinea, the Pacific Islands Regiment needs to focus on key tasks like gathering information, training, and building good relations with local people. Because maps aren't reliable, patrols usually follow known paths or tracks made by local hunters, using a compass and the sun to find their way. Since patrols are often far from help and communication is limited, commanders must plan carefully, bringing enough supplies and making sure they know the route in advance because getting extra help is hard.

Surface warships have historically demonstrated their effectiveness in securing sea lines of communication (SLOCs) and enabling joint operations through amphibious lift, logistic support, and gunfire support. These missions were critical in campaigns such as the Mediterranean and New Guinea during the Second World War.

Surface warships have been important for protecting sea routes and supporting joint military operations, such as moving troops and supplies, providing fire support, and helping with logistics. These roles were especially important in places like the Mediterranean and New Guinea during World War II.

The main aim of the Russian wargame was not to figure out what would happen at the start of the war or to test different strategies, but to support and promote the war plans put forward by the GUGSh. These plans were not popular with many in the Russian Army, so the wargame helped to back them up and make them more acceptable internally.

Professor Greg Austin advocates for a national innovation strategy to develop sovereign cyber war capability and cyber survivability, independent of the United States, to prepare Australia for major military confrontation in the cyber domain. This includes reorganising the Australian Defence Force for cyber-enabled warfare, investing in niche technologies, and renovating military institutions, training, and education for cyber warfare.

Professor Greg Austin suggests that Australia needs its own cyber strategy to be ready for major wars, without relying on the US. He wants the Australian Defence Force to be reorganised for cyber warfare, invest in special technologies, and improve training and education in cyber skills.

The challenge for Australian Defence in adopting emerging autonomous and small-scale technologies is the speed of innovation in this market, which is outpacing Defence's ability to keep pace. Additionally, the entrenched bureaucratic environment and lengthy acquisition programmes may result in outdated or unreliable technology by the time they are procured.

The problem for the Australian Defence in taking on new small and fast-changing technologies, like drones and autonomous systems, is that these technologies are developing quickly. Defence can't keep up because of slow processes and a complicated bureaucracy, which means by the time they buy something, it might already be old or not work well.

The main goal of the RedSix app is to let users connect with each other and get support quickly, without having to go online or share their problems on social media.

However, the speaker notes a gradual erosion of this relationship's equity over time, raising concerns about how long the relationship can remain viable without continued investment.

The speaker says that Australia's security relationship with the US has been like an insurance policy for a long time, going back over 100 years. Australia has worked with the US in many conflicts like Korea, Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan. But the speaker is worried that this relationship is slowly weakening over time and might not last forever if it's not kept strong.

Commodore Sam Bateman made a long-lasting contribution to Australia’s strategic thinking and the development of a more balanced Australian defence capability. He worked tirelessly to broaden understanding of Australia’s geostrategic position and the importance of maritime power to national security. As Director General of the new Maritime Studies Program, he established the organisational structure that became the Sea Power Centre Australia and provided the intellectual content and rigour for a world-class organisation. His efforts also harnessed the energies of many officers and academics to produce works on contemporary and historical naval issues, with a perspective that was not narrowly naval.

Commodore Sam Bateman helped improve Australia’s understanding of its position in the world and the importance of naval power for national security. He worked hard to encourage a more balanced approach to defence planning, focusing on maritime issues. In his role leading the Maritime Studies Program, he set up the foundation for what became the Sea Power Centre Australia and brought together experts to study both modern and historical naval topics. His approach was broad and not limited to just the navy.

The book Middle Power Dreaming is guided by the traditional definition of middle powers as states that pursue multilateral solutions, embrace compromise in international disputes, and demonstrate good international citizenship. It suggests that Australia under the Howard Government was not considered a middle power due to its limited engagement with multilateral institutions, while the Rudd Government was viewed as a middle power because of its greater openness to such forums. However, the book also raises questions about this definition, noting that the Howard Government's actions—such as building defence capability, deploying forces, and leading regional initiatives—suggest a middle power in action, despite its ideological aversion to multilateralism.

The book Middle Power Dreaming looks at how middle powers are usually seen as countries that work with others to solve international problems, try to find middle ground in disputes, and act responsibly on the world stage. It says that Australia under John Howard wasn't really seen as a middle power because he wasn't into working with international groups, but under Kevin Rudd, Australia was considered a middle power because it was more open to that kind of cooperation. Even so, the book questions this view, pointing out that Howard's government did a lot of things—like building up the military, sending troops to places like East Timor and Iraq, and leading a regional security effort—that looked like middle power actions, even if they didn't like working with big international groups.

Navantia Australia's MOU with JLB-Yaran is significant as it supports the development of a supply chain and support partners necessary for the sustainment of naval vessels, including LHDs, DDGs, and AORs. This partnership aligns with the national naval shipbuilding plan, which will require a substantial workforce and professional services to execute sustainment and project work effectively.

Navantia Australia signed an agreement with JLB-Yaran to help build a supply chain and support network for maintaining naval ships like LHDs, DDGs, and AORs. This partnership supports the bigger plan for building and maintaining Australia's navy ships, which needs a lot of skilled workers and support.

The Australian defense and national security industry is currently experiencing a significant brain drain, with high-level capabilities leaving the sector for commercial opportunities. This has been exacerbated by a reduction in defense work and a tendency to outsource to major service providers. There is a concern that this loss of capability will create a resource crunch when the industry attempts to ramp up again, as it may be difficult to re-engage those who have left, particularly if their security clearances have lapsed or they have chosen alternative career paths.

Right now, the defense and national security industry in Australia is struggling with a lot of skilled workers leaving the sector to work in other industries. This has been made worse by less work being available in defense and a tendency to outsource to big companies. There's a worry that when more work becomes available again, it'll be hard to get those people back, especially if they've lost their security clearances or decided they'd rather work in other fields like utilities or banking.

Key risks associated with the use of AI include data integrity issues, biases in AI models, and a broadened attack surface due to AI-specific threats such as data poisoning, prompt injection, and model parameter theft. These risks highlight the importance of governance frameworks to ensure responsible and secure AI deployment.

Using AI can bring some big risks, like problems with the quality of the data used, biased results from the AI, and new ways hackers can attack systems. These include things like tampering with the data, tricking the AI with prompts, or stealing information about how the AI works. It's important to have good rules in place to manage these risks and keep things safe.

The Australian Defence Force leverages the digital capabilities of digital natives while also developing essential soft skills through its training pipeline. This includes building resilience, confidence, self-esteem, negotiation skills, and interpersonal skills. These capabilities are embedded in programs such as the Army, Navy, and Indigenous Pre-Recruit Programs, which aim to prepare recruits for team engagement, communication, and leadership. These skills are critical for future operations and are cultivated to ensure recruits are equipped to lead, negotiate, and deliver outcomes in complex environments.

The Australian Defence Force helps recruits get better at using technology and also works on their people skills. They build confidence, communication, and teamwork through training programs. These programs are especially helpful for people who might need extra support, like those in the Indigenous development programs. The goal is to make sure recruits can work well with others and lead effectively.

Under Phase One, the MGO Branch would have sole responsibility for procurement, research and development, and trials. It would be a non-corps organization staffed by members from relevant army corps with appropriate technical skills and would not control any corps or be directly involved in field operations. The QMG Branch would have no procurement functions and would control all corps responsible for materiel maintenance and movement. It would also be responsible for materiel, movements, and logistic planning. Procurement arrangements would be managed by MGO, with delivery to stock holding depots, after which control would transfer to QMG. The General Staff would prescribe materiel policies, and sponsors would provide advice on specifications and quantities to the procurement branch.

Under the proposed changes, the MGO branch would be in charge of buying, developing, and testing equipment. It would be made up of people from different army units who have the right technical skills, but it wouldn't control any specific unit or take part in field operations. The QMG branch would handle the upkeep and movement of supplies and equipment, and would also plan logistics. It wouldn't be involved in buying things. The MGO would handle the buying process and deliver supplies to storage depots, after which the QMG would take over. The overall army leadership would set the rules for what equipment is needed, and the people who use the equipment would give advice on what to buy and how much.

The author says that Graham made poor decisions because he was ambitious and under a lot of pressure, and that the Australian government didn’t understand the situation in Vietnam well enough to make informed choices.

Adapting foreign ship designs for the Australian Defence Force involves numerous operational and capability challenges, including the need to modify designs to meet Australian requirements such as OH&S standards, paint specifications, and radar systems. These changes are necessary for interoperability with the joint battle management system and to ensure the vessel is equipped with appropriate vertical launch systems (VLS). The process is complex and time-consuming, and there are risks that the resulting vessels may not be fully interoperable or equipped with the best available systems.

Changing foreign ship designs to work in Australia involves a lot of adjustments. For example, things like paint, safety standards, and radar systems need to be updated to meet Australian requirements. These changes are important so the ships can work well with Australia's military systems and have the right weapons. It's a complicated process, and there's a risk that the ships might not all work together properly or have the best equipment.

Clearance Diving Teams (CDTs) have conducted numerous operations in both wartime and non-warlike contexts, including capturing enemy divers, performing high-risk tunnel clearances, and executing deep diving and body recovery tasks in challenging environments. CDT3 received a United States Congressional Unit Citation for its conduct during the Vietnam War, and a CDT deployed to the Gulf War was also awarded a Unit Citation alongside individual decorations. CDTs have supported coalition amphibious operations, UN forces in East Timor, and post-Gulf War ADF operations, including chemical ordnance destruction in Iraq and mine countermeasures in the Persian Gulf. These teams have also been integral to ADF counter-terrorist operations with the SASR for over 15 years.

Clearance Diving Teams have been involved in many important tasks during both war and peace. They've captured enemy divers, cleared dangerous tunnels, and done deep diving in tough conditions like high-altitude dams and after disasters. One team was even given a special award by the US for their work in Vietnam, and another got a similar award during the Gulf War. They've also helped with military planning for amphibious attacks, supported UN missions in East Timor, and worked on removing dangerous weapons in Iraq and other areas. These teams have also been part of anti-terrorism efforts with the SASR for more than 15 years.

Units are made self-supporting by the inclusion of supporting arms and Engineer elements down to a section and a company level, respectively, and by carrying large stocks of supplies such as ammunition, petrol, and food. This ensures self-reliance and supports operational requirements.

To be self-sufficient, units include support weapons and engineering teams at lower levels and carry plenty of supplies like bullets, fuel, and food. This helps them operate independently without relying on external support.

Norman F. Dixon identifies several key problems of leadership in military command, including a serious wastage of human resources and failure to observe economy of force, fundamental conservatism and adherence to outworn tradition, inability to learn from the past, misuse of available technology, rejection of unpalatable information, overestimation of one's own capabilities and underestimation of the enemy, indecisiveness and abdication from decision-making, persistence in a given task despite contrary evidence, failure to exploit situations, inadequate reconnaissance, belief in brute force, preference for frontal assaults, failure to use surprise or deception, undue readiness to find scapegoats for setbacks, suppression or distortion of news from the front, and belief in mystical forces such as fate or bad luck.

Norman F. Dixon points out several issues with military leadership, such as not using resources well, sticking to old traditions, not learning from past mistakes, misusing technology, ignoring information that doesn't fit expectations, being too confident in one's own side and not taking the enemy seriously enough, being indecisive and avoiding making tough choices, continuing with a plan even when it's clearly not working, missing opportunities, not gathering enough information, relying too much on brute force, preferring direct attacks, not using surprise or trickery, blaming others for failures, hiding bad news to keep morale up, and believing in things like bad luck or fate.

The Australian Way of War is based on the strategic fusion of statecraft and strategy through offshore warfare, utilising volunteer forces in coalition operations. This approach has been applied in both unlimited conflicts such as the World Wars and limited wars post-1945. It is characterised by a minimalist military deployment in support of diplomatic positions, with a focus on maintaining economic development and avoiding militarism. The Anzac tradition, rooted in pragmatism, egalitarianism, and mateship, serves as a cultural transmission belt for national values in overseas military operations.

Australia's approach to war has focused on combining diplomacy with military action, especially through overseas operations with allied forces. This method has been used in major wars like World War I and II, as well as smaller conflicts since 1945. Australia has aimed to keep military efforts in line with its diplomatic goals and to avoid letting defense spending harm the economy. The Anzac tradition, which values fairness, teamwork, and practicality, has helped shape how Australian military values are expressed abroad.

Spoken language interaction in human-machine teams can enhance trust and team performance by enabling clear communication between humans and intelligent machines. This can relieve human workload and potentially reduce the number of humans required, such as replacing the co-pilot with a smart aircraft. However, it also introduces the potential for non-work-related conversations, which may lead to anthropomorphisation of the machine.

Using spoken language to interact with smart machines in the Air Force can make it easier for people to work with them, build trust, and reduce the need for as many people. For example, a pilot might talk to an aircraft instead of using controls. This could help with workload, but it might also lead to people chatting with the machines and treating them almost like people.

The protests in Sydney were governed by the Major Events Act 2009, which grants police special powers such as issuing move on orders and stop and search warrants. The protests, intended to march from Town Hall to Parliament House, were restricted due to the latter being a designated restricted zone. The police response included the use of capsicum spray at close range and the aggressive handling of protesters, with some footage showing officers punching demonstrators. These actions have been noted as potentially excessive use of force.

The Sydney protests were managed under a law called the Major Events Act 2009, which allows police to use special powers like telling people to leave an area or searching them. The protests were planned to go from Town Hall to Parliament House, but the latter was a restricted area. Police used pepper spray up close and handled some protesters roughly, with some videos showing officers punching people. These actions have been seen as possibly too forceful.

The MRCVs are designed to function as a 'mothership' for unmanned aerial, surface, and underwater systems, enabling the conduct of naval operations. They are equipped with advanced sensors, weapon systems, and network capabilities to handle a wide range of threats and function as a Command ship. Their advanced automation allows them to operate effectively with a smaller crew compared to similar-sized warships.

The Multi-Role Combat Vessels are built to support unmanned drones and underwater vehicles for naval missions. They have advanced technology for sensing and fighting threats and can act as a command ship. These ships can work well with fewer crew members because of their automated systems.

Military organisational culture can act as an impediment to change, particularly in the face of strategic and political uncertainty. While external conditions such as strategic uncertainty and political imperatives drive the conditions for innovation, internal culture through conservatism and traditionalism tends to shape the nature of change in a way that is more likely to impede innovation. The culture's resistance to change is a response to uncertainty, and leadership plays a key role in either encouraging open debate and experimentation or reinforcing the status quo.

Military culture often makes it hard to bring about change, especially when the future is uncertain. While things like political decisions and big-picture uncertainty can push for new ideas, the culture tends to stick to old ways and resist change. This resistance is a reaction to not knowing what the future holds, and how much change happens often depends on the leaders and whether they support new ideas or stick with the old ways.

text: Putin believed that Ukraine’s society was fragile and would crumble under pressure. These aspects cumulatively served to distort the truth and deliver shaky foundations upon which to assess and manage risk. Finally, operational risk was magnified by the lack of surprise. text: Russian strategy was to seize Kyiv in a ‘coup de main’ assault. A coup de main is defined in US terminology as “an offensive operation that capitalises on surprise and simultaneous execution of supporting operations to achieve success in one swift stroke. This style of assault historically yielded positive results for the former Soviet Union in Hungary in 1956, Czechoslovakia in 1968 and Afghanistan in 1979. According to an accidental leak from a Russian news agency, Putin planned to accomplish the seizure of Kyiv within two days – an astonishing timeline by any reasonable measure. The coup de main assault was contingent on a Russian paratrooper assault on Antonov airfield, reinforced by the rapid deployment of three separate armoured columns. This failed when it encountered the fierce Ukrainian resistance that the Russian forces did not anticipate. The armoured columns required to reinforce the airfield assault were rendered slow or immobile by enemy action as well as maintenance issues and lack of fuel. Ukrainian air defences had not been effectively neutralised and as a result, the Russian Air Force provided inadequate ground support to advancing troops, either due to unwillingness to expose their aircraft to danger or a lack of capability.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: Personnel shortages (particularly infantry), exacerbated their inability to press forward through Ukrainian defences. Battlefield topography impeded the effective use of Russian artillery, and Russian forces became trapped on two routes, unable to retreat or advance effectively. Rendered immobile, their forward forces were in range of Ukrainian artillery while their own artillery and supplies were trapped behind congested friendly forces. The forward elements of the Russian advance had outrun their logistic supply, and were no longer an effective fighting force. Three of the elements identified in JMAP as causes of culmination – loss of combat power, adversary action, and logistics exhaustion – prevented the Russians achieving their primary operational objective of seizing Kyiv. In retrospect this appears to have been unavoidable; an inevitable outcome of the failure to articulate and understand the risk in such an audacious plan. The causes of such a dramatic example of culmination prior to achieving the primary objective are complex. A coup de main requires surprise – which as already outlined was completely neutralised. As previously discussed, planners had an overly optimistic estimate of the combat power of their own forces.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: The Russian peace-time military (and remember Russia at this point was not in a war-time footing – this was merely a ‘special military operation’) is structured for and well-suited to short, high-intensity campaigns characterised by heavy use of artillery. Conversely, it is ill-suited to prolonged, attritional conflict against a determined and well-armed adversary, which is precisely the situation it found itself in after its failed coup de main assault against Kyiv. Significantly, Russian forces failed to concentrate the substantial forces available on the border on their main objective. The invasion proceeded on several disparate axes, without a clear focus and without unity of effort. No single commander oversaw ground forces; instead, each district commander led his own forces, complicating coordination and reducing the effectiveness of the disparate units on the ground. To summarise, although a short, sharp operation to seize Kyiv was the primary objective, Russian forces reached their first operational culminating point well before achieving this aim. Operational reach Operational reach is defined in Australian doctrine as “the distance and duration across which a force element can successfully employ military capabilities.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: Many factors influence and affect operational reach, including weather, terrain, population response and availability of resources from the occupied territory. Operational reach can be extended “through forward positioning of capabilities and resources. This was not possible for Russia, however, as they were invading a nation hostile to their stated military objectives. Furthermore, due to inadequate planning time for lower-level echelons (likely due to the deception of the own people– many units still believed they were merely conducting an exercise), Russian forces struggled to move materiel into forward positions to support ongoing operations. Due to these preconditions, achieving sufficient operational reach necessitated Russian forces controlling occupied terrain and maintaining logistics lines of communication. The first phase of the Russian invasion of Ukraine demonstrates that Russia failed to achieve these two conditions, and as a result their operational reach fell short of that required to achieve their objective. As previously highlighted, in the early phases of the invasion, Russia bet heavily on a short, sharp, coup de main assault. This strategy saw Russia use nearly all its soldiers simultaneously and rapidly enter Ukraine to fight along multiple fronts.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: This not only failed to concentrate force on the main objective, but in their rush to seize Kyiv, Russian forces also skipped protective measures, such as clearing routes of explosives. Significantly, Russia did not achieve air superiority, having failed to substantially degrade the Ukrainian Air Force or conduct effective suppression of air defence. Russian forces advanced at an unsustainable pace, outrunning supply lines. Simultaneously, the melting snow created boggy conditions, confining the Russian armoured columns to highways, making them easy targets to teams of Ukrainian anti-tank missile operators. The tanks and armoured vehicles themselves performed poorly, due to poor maintenance and lack of spare parts, clogging up roadways. Ironically, the armoured columns were both too slow to reinforce the initial assault, and too slow to avoid presenting attractive targets to Ukrainian forces, but too fast for the logistics train to effectively support. As a result of these factors – the dispersion of forces, the slow speed of the logistics supply, the lack of air superiority, and the weather effects, Russian troops were highly vulnerable to ambushes, counterattacks, and severe logistical shortfalls.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: But Ukraine is a very large country, and armour must move quickly and be properly sustained to be effective. The armoured columns prosecuting the coup de main assault were light on infantry, due to persistent personnel shortages. The armoured column was plagued not only by logistic shortages, but the lack of infantry support made them vulnerable to anti-tank missiles. This issue is emblematic of a more serious underlying problem. The Russians forgot - or disregarded - basic lessons of combined arms that were forged in the earlier world wars. These are that tanks are vulnerable without infantry support, tanks and infantry are vulnerable without air cover, and air cover cannot be provided without effective suppression of air defences. Additionally, the Russian Army in previous campaigns typically advanced only after significant shaping artillery fires, which were ‘notably absent’ in the initial stages of the invasion. Russian forces failed at combined arms warfare, and these mistakes were skilfully exploited by Ukrainian forces, bringing the advance to a grinding halt. Operational reach requires control of territory along supply lines. The ‘strength of the rear,’ long a fixation of previous Soviet leaders including Stalin, has been a consistent problem for the Russian forces.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: From early in the campaign, Ukrainian forces were able to infiltrate behind Russian lines and disrupt logistics flows, such as using anti-tank missiles to blow up a Russian train carrying fuel for forward-deployed armoured vehicles. Putin claimed areas of Ukraine in which Ukrainian forces continued to operate with impunity, and although Russian forces were able to seize cities and towns, they lacked the manpower to hold on to these gains. This fact illustrates that Russia’s ability to temporarily hold ground until counter attack or supplies run short is not sustained operational reach. As a counterpoint, Russia has, from the early stages, employed long-range cruise and ballistic missiles against targets deep inside Ukraine. These capabilities have allowed Russia to kinetically affect the battlespace at large distances from their frontlines. However, while devastating to the victims of the strikes and damaging to the Ukrainian economy, this apparent extension of Russian operational reach has not manifestly aided them in controlling key terrain. Conclusion Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine can be reasonably described as ‘bungled’ – poorly planned, poorly executed, and deficient in basic military concepts and elements such as surprise, coordination, and effective combined/joint warfare concepts.
title: An evaluation of the Russian arrangement of military operations during the first phase of the Russo-Ukrainian War

text: The planning of the operation with regards to risk management appears to have been badly deficient, likely due to outdated risk assessment methodologies, inadequate and inaccurate data on own force capability and readiness, and wishful thinking and/or blind ignorance to inconvenient facts. This magnified the operational risk which manifested itself as poor performance on the battlefield. Russian forces faced a much more determined, better prepared and more capable adversary that they had expected and planned for. This factor compounded their mistake in betting on a coup de main assault on Kyiv – a type of operation that requires surprise, speed, and effective coordination of forces to be successful. Russian forces did not possess surprise, their ground and air forces were poorly coordinated, and their three armoured columns, although too fast for their logistics train, were too slow to maintain the operational reach required to enter Kyiv with sufficient fighting forces. As a result, they reached their culminating point prior to achieving the primary military objective.

The Four Days’ Battle of 1666 was strategically significant as it represented an unavoidable consequence of the struggle for control of the North Sea, with the English seeking to intercept Dutch merchant convoys and the Dutch attempting to force the English fleet to remain in the Thames. The battle also marked the first combat test of line-ahead tactics, which became a principal characteristic of naval warfare until the late nineteenth century.

The Four Days’ Battle of 1666 was important because it was a key fight over control of the North Sea. The English wanted to stop Dutch ships bringing goods from overseas, while the Dutch wanted to keep the English fleet stuck in their home waters. It was also the first time ships lined up in a row to fight, a tactic that became common in naval battles for many years.

The Unmanned Netted Lethality concept represents the evolution of Distributed Lethality through the full integration of unmanned systems into the fleet. It envisions hunter-killer Surface Action Groups (SAGs) comprising unmanned underwater vehicles, unmanned surface vehicles, and UAVs under the command of a single manned ship. These platforms form a constellation of sensors and weapons, transforming each ship into a lethal, flexible, and distributed force. This concept relies on the aggressive development and controlled autonomy of unmanned systems, with autonomy levels managed by a manned ship as an extension of the commanding officer’s combat system.

The Unmanned Netted Lethality idea builds on the Distributed Lethality approach by adding more unmanned systems to naval forces. It involves using a mix of unmanned underwater, surface, and air vehicles controlled by a single manned ship. These vehicles work together to create a network of sensors and weapons, making each ship more powerful and adaptable. The concept depends on developing unmanned technology and managing how much control these systems have, with a human ship overseeing operations and adjusting control levels as needed.

Air bases perform three key activities: first, maintaining the physical operational infrastructure to facilitate the generation of effective air power; second, providing personnel and support systems for mission preparation and force sustainment, including garrison services; and third, maintaining organic force protection capabilities that can deploy for expeditionary requirements without compromising main base security.

Implementing recommendations to improve Western military planning frameworks for contemporary political warfare requires a significant shift in strategic thinking, culture, and behaviours. These changes will not be simple or easily implemented, and will take years to mature fully. During this period, the opposition will continue to evolve and adapt, creating an ongoing need for strategic flexibility and responsiveness.

Making the suggested improvements to how Western militaries plan for modern political warfare will require big changes in how people think and act strategically. These changes won't be easy or quick to put in place and will take a long time to fully take effect. In the meantime, the other side will keep changing their tactics, so it's important to stay flexible and keep adapting the planning process.

This is especially true when it is compared to Western governments. An understanding of this period is therefore essential to progressing to why the existing frameworks of planning in Western militaries are currently inadequate. Indeed, the opening two decades of this century have seen ‘the regimes in Moscow and Beijing reaffirm the potential for harnessing offensive political warfare to undermine the US and its Western allies’. Both regimes demonstrate an approach to political warfare which mirrors their domestic environment of oppression, surveillance and police-state mentality, again illuminated further by direct comparison to Western nations. ‘Political warfare’ is used in this context to describe any given government utilising ‘a very wide range of instruments in efforts to persuade, intimidate, coerce, undermine and weaken opponents’ to reach some advantageous end state or effect. This demonstrates that a military responding to political warfare has a wide range of opposing agencies to counter, a key point in assessing how it is contemporarily inadequate from a Western military perspective.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: China, for instance, has the United Front Work Department, the Propaganda Department, the Ministry of State Security—all agencies unified under the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) with the intent of unifying political warfare actions rather than a loose collection of isolated activities. Russia, too, has strongly nationalistic agencies working in cooperation towards an overarching strategic goal. Both countries in their approach to political warfare utilise their militaries as one component of the ways and means to these strategic ends, with no significant equivalent from Western nations over this same contemporary time period. The methods used by China and Russia in contemporary political warfare are of vital importance in determining how Western militaries can effectively counter them. To this end, modern examples are most demonstrative of these methods and will be assessed here. In Russia, Vladimir Putin’s regime has seen many political advances as a result of contemporary political warfare. For example, Russia’s defence in depth has improved as a result of coercion on neighbouring states in Eastern Europe and the Baltic region to create a geographical buffer zone.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: COG analysis has become more prevalent in operational design of Western military doctrine since the late 1990s. This is the same timeframe previously described of the increase in contemporary political warfare from Russia and China. This now leads to the crux of the issue of why these theoretical and procedural frameworks are left wanting in dealing with contemporary political warfare—the attachment of the West to a definitive, kinetic battle. There is a Western way of war, which the above doctrine is firmly anchored to—one that is ‘birthed by the citizen soldiers of classical Greece’. It is one which favours a binary concept of peace or war, which matches Western culture and perceptions. This is further evidenced by the definition of operational art, which is of vital importance to Western doctrine—‘combat actions forged into an ensemble to provide the creative tactical material for extensive operations united by strategy’. The emphasis and reliance on combat and kinetic actions is to be noted, and further creates the overall picture of a doctrine of military campaigns with clear delineations between war and peace.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: There is nothing incorrect or contradictory to this approach per se, and it is a continually evolving process through military academic study and experience. Where it falls short, however, is when it is viewed through the lens of contemporary political warfare, which by definition does not have such stark demarcation of war and peace and instead fits intentionally in between the two. This creates new difficulties which are not readily fixable by this extant doctrine and plays into the development and success of the contemporary political warfare facing Western democracies and their militaries. This approach to doctrine and military campaigns is relatively uniform across Western nations and not unique to Australia. For example, following the collapse of the Soviet Union and the resultant end of the Cold War, the US Army’s doctrine manual stated: ‘The American people expect decisive victory—they prefer quick resolution’ and ‘their values and expectations to be met. This is a strategic culture which repeats across Western nations, and in contrast to the aforementioned authoritarian approach of grey-zone warfare or such actions that fall short of war.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: The end result here is an inability of Western militaries to clearly define their ends when the opponent is non-traditional and asymmetric by intent. This in turn then enables, and indeed perpetuates, a situation of military planning processes not being effectively able to counter contemporary political warfare, since the opponent centre of gravity is obtuse and variable. Amongst these Western nations, the United Kingdom is perhaps the outlying exception since their recent doctrinal developments have included concepts of minimising the intent of a decisive victory or seeking a formal surrender. Instead, the newer doctrine includes focusing on concepts like population opinion, synergies between non-military forces and military capability measures beyond conventional combat. These issues will be explored further in the next section of how the existing theoretical and procedural frameworks can be improved with respect to the demands of contemporary political warfare. The disadvantageous mismatch of Western militaries and contemporary political warfare is perhaps best summated by analysing the Gerasimov model—Russia’s 2013 doctrine created by General Valery Gerasimov, the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces. In this planning framework, there are six clearly defined phases of conflict.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: This is the more comprehensive component—in not limiting the assessment inputs to military planners but instead ensuring the process is more inclusive of non-military agencies. The expected outcome of this approach is to generate a logical flow of planning elements to lead to decisive points for the commander which encompass the required input of all elements of contemporary political warfare. The systematic aspect of how this can occur is ultimately beyond the scope of this essay, other than to highlight that the extant planning process requires a restructure to enable this broader input. Another key reason for the need of a more comprehensive military planning model is to counter the limitations previously described of the West’s strong sense of delineation between war and peace, or conflict and non-conflict. Planning, by its nature, requires revision and updates based on continuous assessment and reassessment, and the current escalating use of actions short of warfare are not being appropriately addressed. The future result of this is difficult to determine, but it is not unreasonable to question if escalating political warfare will drive us to violent conflict.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: This outcome can be avoided, or at least have violent conflict brought more towards the West’s strategic control, by decoupling military planning from the stark delineation of conflict or not, similar to what Russia and China have firmly grasped over the last 20 years. To this end, the following recommendations for improvements to Western military planning and conduct of campaigns will increase both the practicability of operations and their relevance to contemporary political warfare. Firstly, in recognising that military planning is a tool of a whole-of-government approach, military planning should include more civilian representatives from other government agencies to enhance understanding and coordination. Should this not occur, there will likely be a perpetuation of the inward military vision of kinetic actions or not, and a risk of plans that do not effectively reach the required end state of countering contemporary political warfare. Secondly, and closely attached to the first recommendation as a corollary, there should be greater incentivisation and training for military representatives within other government agencies. In Australia, for instance, more senior military personnel in agencies such as Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Home Affairs, Health and other such departments will enhance coordination and mutual understanding.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: This will further aid the comprehensiveness of military planning, provide greater scope of available logistics and courses of action, and remove the inward view of the military only viewing problems with a militaristic mindset. The third recommendation to amend a shortcoming in Western militaries’ frameworks is to enable cooperative military-government agencies to focus on ‘critical information requirements’ surrounding political warfare threats. Western nations within Europe have begun to make progress on this issue, with a recent request for further intelligence on Russian financial involvement with political donations, leaders and parties. These sorts of intelligence elements will further enhance the overall picture for inputs to comprehensive military planning, as well as aid the whole-of-government in terms of policy-making decisions. This point is worth emphasising since the military can achieve a side effect of embracing this recommendation by helping shape government policy—a considerable benefit to the relevance and authority of any government agency. The fourth and last recommendation with respect to Western militaries’ planning is to emphasise the need for proactivity in utilising their forces in areas which are deemed susceptible to foreign persuasion through political warfare.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

text: The benefits of this approach are twofold for military planning—firstly, it helps reduce the global effect of opposition political warfare activities, and secondly, it provides the Western militaries with experience and operational impact to adapt to the demands of contemporary political warfare. This recommendation is particularly important in the development of experience for military planners, in particular if the aforementioned recommendations see a redevelopment of sorts of military planning. It is appreciated and understood that any new processes will take time to become familiar and be of useful practical application. Therefore, taking a proactive stance of utilising it will indeed see multiple benefits for the improvement of both the theoretical and procedural frameworks. Conclusion Contemporary political warfare is an ever-present and evolving issue faced by Western governments. It is therefore of paramount importance for militaries to also evolve in how they can respond to it. As has been demonstrated, the present planning frameworks have multiple limitations in allowing Western militaries to adapt to these demands, and the end result is a strategic disadvantage to Western nations and their populace.
title: War or Peace? That’s So Last Century

The 'Blue Pacific' idea is important because it helps the Pacific Islands see themselves as a united region rather than many separate islands. This shared identity builds unity and strength, allowing them to work together on global issues and make sure outside countries work with them, not against them.
